<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    One of the biggest obstacles to building a large scale quantum computer is the high qubit cost of protecting quantum information. For two-dimensional architectures, the surface code has long been the leading candidate quantum memory, but can require upwards of a thousand physical qubits per logical qubit to reach algorithmically-relevant logical error rates. In this work, we introduce a hierarchical memory formed from surface codes concatenated into high-density parity check codes. These yoked surface codes are arrayed in a rectangular grid, with parity checks (yokes) measured along each row, and optionally along each column, using lattice surgery. Our construction assumes no additional connectivity beyond a nearest-neighbor square qubit grid operating at a physical error rate of 10
                    <jats:sup>−3</jats:sup>
                    . At algorithmically-relevant logical error rates, yoked surface codes use as few as one-third the number of physical qubits per logical qubit as standard surface codes, enabling moderate-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memories in two dimensions.
                  </jats:p>
title: Yoked surface codes

items.abstract: <jats:p>This inaugural lecture by Professor Oluwakemi Mary Adekile critically examines the inequities embedded in Nigeria’s matrimonial property regime, particularly under statutory marriage. While customary marriage practices have received significant judicial scrutiny and reform, statutory marriage remains largely stagnant, perpetuating structural injustices in property distribution. Drawing on case law, statutory provisions, and socio-legal analysis, the lecture interrogates the role of family law, judicial discretion, and human rights in shaping matrimonial property rights. It highlights how property ownership functions as a source of economic security and autonomy, yet discriminatory legal frameworks continue to disadvantage women, leaving spouses “unequally yoked” despite vows of shared possessions. Through examples such as Toyin Arajulu v Solomon Monday, Professor Adekile illustrates the potential of judicial discretion to advance fairness, while lamenting legislative inertia and limited judicial activism. The lecture ultimately calls for urgent reform of family law to ensure equitable distribution of matrimonial property, arguing that neglecting this domain undermines justice, social cohesion, and sustainable development.</jats:p>
title: Unequally Yoked: Matrimonial Property Rights Not A Promise Of Law
